subject: Physiology
summary: Sensory receptors convert physical or chemical stimuli into nerve signals. Their properties (threshold, adaptation, modality) determine how patients perceive pain, temperature, touch, and proprioception, guiding diagnosis and treatment.

sections.p: Sensory receptors are specialised cells or nerve endings that detect external or internal stimuli and generate receptor potentials that trigger action potentials.
b: Two main types: free‑ending (pain, temperature) and encapsulated (touch, vibration).
Receptor potential is graded; once threshold is reached, an action potential fires.

sections.p: Stimulus energy (mechanical, thermal, chemical) opens ion channels, producing a receptor potential. If the depolarisation reaches threshold, voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels fire an action potential that travels along a labelled line to the CNS.
b: Thermoreceptors: TRP channels respond to heat (>43 °C) or cold (<15 °C).
Chemoreceptors: detect pH, CO₂, or specific chemicals (e.g., carotid body).

t.b: What is the patient’s detection threshold for vibration? Abnormal high threshold suggests large‑fiber neuropathy.
Does the sensory nerve conduct normally? Slowed velocity indicates demyelination or axonal loss.

sections.p: Receptor sensitivity adapts to sustained stimuli (adaptation) and can be modulated by inflammatory mediators, hormones, and central descending pathways.
b: Rapid adaptation: Meissner’s corpuscles – useful for detecting change.
Slow adaptation: Merkel cells – important for static pressure.

sections.p: Damage or dysfunction of receptors produces sensory loss, dysesthesia, or pain syndromes. Patterns of loss help localise the lesion.
b: Peripheral neuropathy: loss of vibration and proprioception (large‑fiber).
Small‑fiber neuropathy: burning pain, loss of temperature sensation.
Central deafferentation: loss of all modalities below the lesion.

t.a: Skin biopsy for intra‑epidermal nerve fibre density
t.b: Is small‑fiber loss present? Reduced density confirms small‑fiber neuropathy, especially in diabetes or HIV.

sections.p: Understanding receptor types guides assessment of pain, balance, and reflexes, and informs treatment choices such as neuropathic analgesics or physiotherapy.
b: Pain that is burning, shooting, or allodynic points to small‑fiber or central sensitisation.
Loss of proprioception increases fall risk – important in low‑resource settings where assistive devices are scarce.

sections.p: Key points examiners test: receptor types, adaptation, clinical patterns of sensory loss, and appropriate investigations.
b: Labelled line principle – each fibre carries one modality.
Differentiate peripheral neuropathy (stocking‑glove) from spinal cord lesions (level‑wise loss).

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of all sensation in a limb (possible acute spinal cord compression).
Rapidly progressive peripheral neuropathy with weakness (possible Guillain‑Barré or toxic neuropathy).
Severe unexplained burning pain with autonomic signs (possible acute small‑fiber neuropathy from infection).

faq.q: Why do some receptors adapt quickly while others do not?
faq.a: Fast‑adapting receptors detect changes; slow‑adapting receptors signal sustained pressure, reflecting their ion‑channel kinetics.

faq.q: Can a normal nerve conduction study rule out neuropathy?
faq.a: No; it assesses large‑fiber function. Small‑fiber neuropathy may have normal studies and requires QST or skin biopsy.

faq.q: How does diabetes affect sensory receptors?
faq.a: Hyperglycaemia damages small‑fiber endings first, causing loss of temperature and pain sensation, then large‑fiber loss later.

exam: Explain how receptor potential differs from an action potential and why a threshold is needed.
Describe the clinical examination findings that differentiate large‑fiber from small‑fiber neuropathy.
List three investigations for a patient with suspected peripheral neuropathy and state what each answers.
